name: Refugee Council: resettlement, children's services, integration and destitution (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: refugees and people seeking asylum in England, helped where they live now.
summary: The Refugee Council is the UK's national refugee charity; this model covers its four service lines in the year to March 2025 (£12.25m): casework for about 1,700 refugees resettled with English councils, advice, housing and asylum-support help for about {{row:households_reached}} people seeking asylum and newly recognised refugees, and advice, reception and youth work for 7,022 separated children and young people. It comes to about {{result}} years of healthy life per $1,000 (plausible range {{range}}): the help is valued at its money and wellbeing worth to clients in the UK, who consume many times what the people overseas aid reaches do, and councils and the Home Office would commission much of it from someone else. About half the result is resettlement (benefits and earnings brought forward), two-fifths integration and destitution (support secured, homelessness averted) and the rest children's services, including children moved from adult hotels into care after age-dispute challenges. The biggest uncertainties are what the help is worth to each client and how much others would have given anyway; every branch is discounted for missing data, since no outcome is measured against a comparison group.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: The outcome in the family's shared unit, per dollar.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

story.sentence: Every **{cost_total / people_reached|$}** pays for casework, advice and youth work that helps one refugee, person seeking asylum or separated child in the UK.

rows.label: Resettlement, year to 31 March 2025 (£)

source.title: British Refugee Council (Refugee Council), Trustees Annual Report and Accounts for the year ended 31 March 2025 (audited; Charity Commission register, charity 1014576)

rows.explainer: Casework for refugees resettled to England under government schemes (the Afghan resettlement programmes, the UK Resettlement Scheme, Homes for Ukraine) in partnership with local authorities in Yorkshire and Humberside, Hertfordshire and Lewisham, and the transitional housing service for Afghans at Catterick. All restricted money, mostly council contracts (Leeds City Council £4.1m, note 5a).

rows.label: Children's Services, year to 31 March 2025 (£)

source.title: British Refugee Council (Refugee Council), Trustees Annual Report and Accounts for the year ended 31 March 2025 (audited; Charity Commission register, charity 1014576)

rows.explainer: Separated children and young people: the reception service at Dover for children arriving alone by small boat (a Home Office contract, £2.2m in note 5a), the Children's Advice and Support Service and Youth AdviceLine, regional youth advice teams, the Youth Service (peer mentoring, events, casework) and age-dispute work.

rows.label: Integration, year to 31 March 2025 (£)

source.title: British Refugee Council (Refugee Council), Trustees Annual Report and Accounts for the year ended 31 March 2025 (audited; Charity Commission register, charity 1014576)

rows.explainer: Support for people seeking asylum and newly recognised refugees moving from asylum support into mainstream housing, benefits, health care, English and work: the asylum project teams in hotels, Infoline, the Refugee Advice Project and Private Rental Scheme in London, the Barnsley Refugee Advice Project and employment programmes.

rows.label: Destitution, year to 31 March 2025 (£)

source.title: British Refugee Council (Refugee Council), Trustees Annual Report and Accounts for the year ended 31 March 2025 (audited; Charity Commission register, charity 1014576)

rows.explainer: Immediate personal support and advice for people at risk of destitution (the accounts' definition, p. 38). Counted with Integration in the adults' branch: the same clients (people refused asylum support, newly recognised refugees whose support has ended).

rows.explainer: Resettled refugees and newly recognised refugees together; the report doesn't split them.

source.title: British Refugee Council (Refugee Council), Trustees Annual Report and Accounts for the year ended 31 March 2025 (audited; Charity Commission register, charity 1014576)

rows.explainer: Help through the asylum process, asylum support, health care and legal referrals, in hotels, at drop-ins and by phone (Infoline).

rows.label: Children and young people supported by Youth Services

source.title: British Refugee Council (Refugee Council), Trustees Annual Report and Accounts for the year ended 31 March 2025 (audited; Charity Commission register, charity 1014576)
source.quote: We supported 7,022 children and young people last year.

rows.explainer: Most arrived alone; over 90% under 18.

rows.label: Share of Refugee Services' clients who came through resettlement schemes
rows.explainer: Judgment 40% (25-60%): the report counts resettled and newly recognised refugees together (4,320). Resettlement spends more than twice Integration's money (£5.3m against £2.4m) but its casework is far more intensive per person (councils commission a caseworker per family for a year or more), while Integration's clients include many one-off advice contacts and all 3,927 asylum clients. 40% gives about £3,100 a resettled client and about £430 an integration or destitution client.

rows.label: Resettled refugees supported
People seeking asylum and newly recognised refugees supported (integration and destitution)
People per household
rows.explainer: The shared UK figure; it only turns the count of people into households and back (people_reached is the count of people either way). The report counts people ("In 2024/2025 we supported: 15,203 refugees and People seeking asylum", p. 6); the three groups add up to 15,269, so about 66 people used two services and are counted in each. What a family client's help does for the rest of the family is left out (a small understatement).

rows.label: Clients supported in the modelled programmes, in households
People reached
Cost per person reached
rows.explainer: Context: compare the IRC's US resettlement services, the nearest peer, about $1,400 a person.

rows.label: Benefits and entitlements a resettled client gets sooner or wouldn't have got (£ a year)
rows.explainer: Judgment £400 (£150-900): caseworkers set up Universal Credit, child benefit and housing claims, bank accounts and eVisas. Universal Credit's standard allowance for a single person over 25 was £393 a month in 2024/25 and the first payment comes five weeks after a claim; getting claims in on arrival and fixing refusals brings roughly a month of benefits forward, more for families, nothing for clients who would have managed. Councils' own resettlement teams and the schemes' funding cover the housing itself.

rows.label: Share of resettled clients whose job comes sooner thanks to the employment help
rows.explainer: Judgment 4% (1-10%): the report describes job clubs, work experience, re-accreditation for medical professionals and partnerships with IKEA, Starbucks and the NHS but publishes no placements; the IRC's European programmes placed 459 people from 88,091 served (0.5%).

rows.label: Earnings brought forward by a job found sooner (£)
rows.explainer: Judgment £5,500 (£2,500-11,000): about three months' earlier start at the National Living Wage (£11.44 an hour from April 2024, 37.5 hours a week, about £5,600), less the Universal Credit withdrawn as earnings rise (counted at gross pay here, since the benefit saved goes back to taxpayers). Most would find work anyway, so only the months gained count.

rows.label: Value received per resettled client in the year (US$)
rows.explainer: Benefits brought forward plus earnings brought forward, averaged over every resettled client. Caseworkers' time is counted only through what it brings, not again at its cost.

rows.label: Average consumption per person in the UK by the household survey (US$)
rows.explainer: The UK's national-accounts consumption per person × the shared survey-to-national-accounts ratio (a shared conversion, not thin data).

rows.label: Resettled refugees' consumption per person, as a share of the average
rows.explainer: The shared figure for refugees and people seeking asylum in the UK (18%, 10-30%): resettled refugees in their first year live on Universal Credit with council-arranged housing, as newly recognised refugees do. Read by every model of help to them, so they value the same people the same way.

rows.label: Resettled refugees' consumption per person (US$)
Years the help keeps its money value
rows.explainer: One year by construction: benefits and earnings brought forward are counted once, in the year.

rows.label: ln(consumption) gain per resettled client, discounted
rows.explainer: The site's one log-income scale at the clients' own consumption.

rows.label: Share of integration and destitution clients whose asylum support or benefit claim the help changes
rows.explainer: Judgment 15% (5-30%): the teams help people apply for asylum support, get it reinstated after an incorrect refusal or eviction notice, and make Universal Credit claims before asylum support ends 28 days after a grant (pp. 9-11); most clients come for advice, information or a referral that changes no payment. Anchor: the asylum project and Infoline are advice services, where a minority of contacts are casework.

rows.label: Weeks of support or benefit secured for those clients
rows.explainer: Judgment 4 weeks (2-10): a claim made or a refusal overturned sooner, a gap between asylum support ending and Universal Credit's first payment (five weeks after a claim) closed, or support kept that would have stopped.

rows.label: Value of a week of the support secured (£)

source.title: GOV.UK, Asylum support: what you'll get
source.quote: You'll usually get £49.18 for each person in your household.

rows.explainer: Judgment £60 (£45-95): asylum support is £49.18 a week for self-catered accommodation (gov.uk) and comes with the housing; Universal Credit's standard allowance for a single adult over 25 was £393 a month (about £90 a week) in 2024/25; most clients changed are in the asylum system.

rows.label: Value of free prescriptions and dental care secured, averaged over every client (£)
rows.explainer: Judgment £15 (£5-40): HC2 certificates (free prescriptions, dental treatment and sight tests) and help reaching a GP or dentist (p. 9), worth tens of pounds a year to the clients who get them, averaged over everyone counted. The health gain itself is in dalys_averted_per_person.

rows.label: Support and entitlements secured per integration or destitution client (£)
rows.explainer: The clients whose payments change × the weeks × a week's value, plus health access averaged over everyone: about £50 a client.

rows.label: Integration and destitution clients' consumption per person, as a share of the average
rows.explainer: The shared figure for people in the UK asylum system ({{row:int_consumption_share}}, 10-30%): asylum support of £49.18 a week with housing provided, a little more for newly recognised refugees on Universal Credit. Read by every model of help to them, so they value the same people the same way.

rows.label: Integration and destitution clients' consumption per person (US$)
ln(consumption) gain per integration or destitution client from support secured
rows.explainer: One year's value against a year's consumption.

rows.label: Share of integration and destitution clients whose homelessness the help averts
rows.explainer: Judgment 4% (1-10%): the Refugee Advice Project and Private Rental Scheme help newly recognised refugees find housing before asylum support ends, and the teams challenged councils to meet their relief duty (p. 11); the report gives no count. Newly recognised refugees are a few thousand of the 6,500 clients; refugee homelessness after the 28-day move-on period is common (the government's own evaluation of the 56-day pilot, 2026), but most clients come for other help and many would have been housed by the council anyway.

rows.label: Weeks of homelessness averted for those clients
rows.explainer: Judgment 8 weeks (3-20): the time a newly recognised refugee without a home spends in a night shelter, sofa-surfing or on the street before a council or private tenancy (Abdul's story, p. 11: a week from referral to a place after sleeping rough).

rows.label: Value of a roof for a night to the person housed (£)
rows.explainer: Judgment £18 (£10-30): what the cheapest room costs, the value to someone who would otherwise go without: a room in a shared house outside London rents for about £400-700 a month (£13-23 a night), more in London; never the cost of the services that find it.

rows.label: Years of homelessness averted per client so helped
ln(consumption) gain per client so helped
rows.explainer: A roof for those weeks only: t × ln(1 + a year's worth of the nightly value ÷ b), the same as t × ln(1 + v ÷ (b × t)) with v the value of the t years' nights (domestic-services family), at the clients' own consumption.

rows.label: Of those whose homelessness is averted, share who would have slept rough
rows.explainer: Judgment 30% (10-60%): Abdul slept rough; most homeless refugees sofa-surf or go to night shelters first. Anchor: in the London CHAIN count, people leaving asylum accommodation are a growing share of new rough sleepers, but most homeless refugees are housed by councils in temporary accommodation.

rows.label: Excess yearly death rate of sleeping rough
rows.explainer: Judgment 1% a year (0.3-3%): people sleeping rough in England and Wales die at a mean age of about 45 (ONS, deaths of homeless people), and cohort studies of people sleeping rough find death rates several times their age group's; for young adults in good health at arrival, about a percentage point a year above their peers', the cause being the street (exposure, assault, drugs) rather than who ends up there.

rows.label: Deaths averted per integration or destitution client (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: Clients housed × the share who would have slept rough × the weeks × the excess death rate. Small next to the money value; the services don't otherwise avert deaths (the therapy model counts suicides).

rows.label: Share of the deaths averted that are of children under five
rows.explainer: Judgment 1% (0-3%): rough sleeping is almost all single adults; families are housed by councils under their statutory duties.

rows.label: Of the deaths averted at five or older, share aged 5 to 14
rows.explainer: Judgment 1% (0-3%): children are housed with their families or by children's services.

rows.label: Of the deaths averted at 15 or older, share aged 15 to 49
rows.explainer: Judgment 90% (80-97%): people seeking asylum and newly recognised refugees are mostly young adults; the rest at 50-74.

rows.label: Value of a death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: GiveWell's moral weights by the age band of each death, times your value of a life: the site's one value of a death.

rows.label: Illness averted per integration or destitution client, in DALYs (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: Judgment 0.0005 (0-0.002) healthy years a client: help registering with a GP, HC2 certificates, dental treatment with a partner group of dentists (p. 9); averaged over everyone, small next to the money's value. Mental health care is in the therapy model.

rows.label: Life satisfaction gained per child or young person while the effect lasts (points, 0-10)
rows.explainer: Judgment 0.1 points (0.02-0.3) for everyone counted: a safe place on arrival at Dover, advice on the asylum claim and on getting a solicitor, school and social care, peer mentoring and activities. No controlled evaluation of such services exists (the Refugee Council doesn't survey children under 16). Anchor: group programmes cut loneliness by 0.27 SD (Shekelle et al. 2024); separated children are among the most isolated, and most get one-to-one advice. Age disputes are counted separately below.

rows.label: Years the children's wellbeing gain lasts
rows.explainer: Judgment half a year (3 months to 1.5 years): the advice and activities last while a child is a client, typically months until care and school are arranged; longer for Youth Service members.

rows.label: WELLBYs per child or young person, discounted
rows.explainer: Point-years, discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Children a year taken into council care after the Refugee Council challenges an adult age assessment

source.title: The National, Report finds 'flawed' UK age assessments a risk to child migrants (23 January 2024), reporting the Refugee Council, Helen Bamber Foundation and Humans for Rights Network report Forced Adulthood
source.quote: 406 children have since had their age accepted by local authorities

rows.explainer: Judgment 70 a year (30-150): the report says the teams challenge incorrect age assessments and two councils' practice (pp. 7-8) without a count. Anchor: the Refugee Council's joint report found 1,300 children placed in adult accommodation or detention between January 2022 and June 2023, of whom 406 had since had their age accepted by local authorities, many with the help of the Refugee Council, Humans for Rights Network and solicitors.

rows.label: Life satisfaction gained by a child moved from adult accommodation into care (points)
rows.explainer: Judgment 1 point (0.3-2): a child alone in an adult asylum hotel or detention, at risk of abuse and out of school, moved into foster care or supported accommodation with a social worker and school. Anchor: in panel surveys of refugees in Germany and Australia, insecure housing and separation from family are among the largest falls in life satisfaction (about a point).

rows.label: Years the move into care is brought forward
rows.explainer: Judgment half a year (2 months to 1.5 years): many would be recognised as children later, at a tribunal or when a council assesses them; the challenge shortens the time in adult accommodation.

rows.label: WELLBYs from age-dispute challenges (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: Children × the gain × the years brought forward, discounted. The years brought forward are already the difference the help makes, so the branch's counterfactual doesn't apply to it again.

rows.label: Resettlement: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: Judgment 0.7 (0.4-0.9): the money brought forward is judged from how the benefits work, with no evaluation of the Refugee Council's casework.

rows.label: Resettlement: share of the outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: Judgment 40% (20-70%): the councils that commission the casework (Leeds, Hertfordshire, Lewisham) must support resettled families under the schemes' funding and would commission another provider or do it in-house; what remains is the difference in quality and the clients another provider wouldn't reach as fast.

rows.label: Integration and destitution: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: Judgment 0.7 (0.4-0.9): the money, housing and health gains are judged with no evaluation. A check, not a trial: in repeated surveys of about 800 clients, 31% of asylum clients and 55% of others reported more confidence dealing with unexpected events, against 6% and 14% worse (p. 14), with no comparison group.

rows.label: Integration and destitution: share of the outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: Judgment 60% (40-80%): advice for people seeking asylum is scarce (the Home Office's advice contractor, Migrant Help, works by phone; local refugee charities are few outside cities), but some clients would get the same help from another charity, a council or friends.

rows.label: Children's services: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: Judgment 0.6 (0.4-0.9), below the other branches: both the general gain and the age-dispute gain are judgments with no outcome data from the children.

rows.label: Children's services: share of the general outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: Judgment 50% (30-80%): councils have duties to children in need and the Home Office would contract another provider for the Dover reception service; independent advice and youth work for separated children have few other providers.

rows.label: This charity's share of the resources behind the outcome
rows.explainer: Judgment 85% (70-100%): volunteers run many groups and activities (Mo's English and job help, p. 10), partners give dental treatment and work placements (IKEA, Starbucks, the NHS), and councils and solicitors act on the referrals (Convention 2). Their money is not in the cost.

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Delivery adjustment
rows.explainer: Judgment 85% (70-95%), all branches: some clients counted came once or dropped out, and the summer 2024 attacks on asylum hotels and the eVisa change disrupted services mid-case.

rows.label: Leverage and funging
rows.explainer: Judgment 0.9 (0.75-1.05): 76% of these lines' spending is restricted (£9.3m of £12.25m) (council and Home Office contracts, grants); a donor's unrestricted pound mostly tops up children's services and integration, where contracts leave gaps, and may partly replace money a funder would otherwise give.

rows.label: Resettlement: counted less for missing outcome data
rows.explainer: Thin: clients counted (and split from the integration clients by a judgment), the money brought forward judged with no evaluation. Counted less by the shared slider (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: Integration and destitution: counted less for missing outcome data
rows.explainer: Thin: clients counted, the value and the homelessness averted judged with no evaluation. Counted less by the shared slider.

rows.label: Children's services: counted less for missing outcome data
rows.explainer: Thin: children counted, the effect judged with no outcome data. Counted less by the shared slider.

rows.label: Resettlement: adjustments combined
rows.formula: res_evidence_adj * res_counterfactual_adj * attribution_share * implementation_adj * leverage_funging_adj * res_missing_data_adj

rows.label: Integration and destitution: adjustments combined
rows.formula: int_evidence_adj * int_counterfactual_adj * attribution_share * implementation_adj * leverage_funging_adj * int_missing_data_adj

rows.label: Children's services: adjustments combined
rows.formula: chd_evidence_adj * chd_counterfactual_adj * attribution_share * implementation_adj * leverage_funging_adj * chd_missing_data_adj

rows.label: Side effect: volunteers' own wellbeing and neighbours' contact with refugees
rows.explainer: The groups and activities bring local volunteers and neighbours together with refugees (beach trips, allotments, football, Mo and Andy, p. 10): a small wellbeing gain for the volunteers and less hostility locally. 2% (0-6%) of the modelled result.

rows.label: Side effect: help that replaces informal support
rows.explainer: Clients with a caseworker lean less on relatives, faith groups and community organisations, which would have given part of the same help; the counterfactuals count other providers, not this. -2% (-5% to 0).

rows.label: Benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: The signed side effects above, each read at the shared side-effect weight. The policy work that draws on the services' evidence is in charityevals' advocacy model of the Refugee Council, not here.

rows.label: Resettlement: income gained, in units of value (after adjustments)
Integration and destitution: support secured, homelessness and deaths averted, in units of value (after adjustments)
rows.formula: int_people * ((int_ln_gain + int_homeless_averted_share * int_homeless_ln_gain) * $uov_per_ln_consumption + deaths_averted_per_person * value_per_death) * int_total_adj

rows.label: Income gained and deaths averted, in GiveWell units of value
rows.explainer: Both money branches, each after its own adjustments.

rows.label: Income gained and deaths averted, in healthy years
rows.explainer: The bridge from UoV into healthy years (docs/normalization.md 2.6): fixed, don't edit.

rows.label: Life satisfaction gained, in WELLBYs (after adjustments)
rows.explainer: The children's branch: everyone's general gain and the age-dispute gain, after the branch's adjustments, the age-dispute part without the counterfactual (its years brought forward already are the difference the help makes).

rows.label: Life satisfaction gained, in healthy years
rows.explainer: The bridge from WELLBYs into healthy years (docs/normalization.md 2.6): fixed, don't edit.

rows.label: Healthy years counted directly (after adjustments)
Resettlement's healthy years
rows.explainer: Through the fixed bridge, for the weights below.

rows.label: Integration and destitution's units of value, in healthy years
rows.explainer: The fixed bridge (normalization.md 2.6), for the weights below.

rows.label: Integration and destitution's healthy years
rows.explainer: Money, deaths and health, for the weights below.

rows.label: Children's services' healthy years
rows.explainer: For the weights below.

rows.label: Resettlement before adjustments
Integration and destitution before adjustments
Children's services before adjustments
Evidence adjustment (outcome-weighted average)
rows.formula: (res_dalys_unadjusted * res_evidence_adj + int_dalys_unadjusted * int_evidence_adj + chd_dalys_unadjusted * chd_evidence_adj) / (res_dalys_unadjusted + int_dalys_unadjusted + chd_dalys_unadjusted)
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only: each branch applies its own row, weighted by its outcome before adjustments in healthy years.

rows.label: Share that wouldn't have happened anyway (outcome-weighted average)
rows.formula: (res_dalys_unadjusted * res_counterfactual_adj + int_dalys_unadjusted * int_counterfactual_adj + chd_dalys_unadjusted * chd_counterfactual_adj) / (res_dalys_unadjusted + int_dalys_unadjusted + chd_dalys_unadjusted)
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only: each branch applies its own row, weighted by its outcome before adjustments in healthy years.

rows.label: Counted less for missing outcome data (outcome-weighted average)
rows.formula: (res_dalys_unadjusted * res_missing_data_adj + int_dalys_unadjusted * int_missing_data_adj + chd_dalys_unadjusted * chd_missing_data_adj) / (res_dalys_unadjusted + int_dalys_unadjusted + chd_dalys_unadjusted)
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only: each branch applies its own row, weighted by its outcome before adjustments in healthy years.

rows.label: All adjustments combined (outcome-weighted average)
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only: each branch applies its own row, weighted by its outcome before adjustments in healthy years.

rows.label: Years of healthy life
rows.explainer: The three branches' healthy years, each already adjusted, plus the side effects.
